title: Thermodynamics
summary: ## Basic ideas
A thermodynamic system is described by its state variables: pressure, volume and temperature.
Thermal equilibrium: two bodies in contact exchange no heat when they are at the same temperature.
Zeroth law: if A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in equilibrium with each other. This defines temperature, which decides the direction of heat flow.
A system is in thermodynamic equilibrium when it is in thermal, mechanical and chemical equilibrium at the same time.
## Heat, work and internal energy
Heat is energy in transit because of a temperature difference, measured in joules. 1 cal = 4.186 J and 1 kcal ≈ 4186 J (J is the mechanical equivalent of heat).

Internal energy U is the total kinetic and potential energy of the molecules. It is a function of state and does not depend on how the state was reached. For an ideal gas, U depends only on temperature. Heat is closely associated with the random kinetic energy of molecules.
Work done by a gas is W = ∫P dV, the area under the P–V (indicator) diagram. In an isobaric process W = P(V₂ − V₁).
## First law
ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW, where ΔQ is the heat supplied, ΔU the rise in internal energy and ΔW the work done by the system. Work done on the system increases U.
Examples: 110 J supplied with ΔU = 40 J gives W = 70 J. Absorbing 2000 J while doing 500 J of work gives ΔU = 1500 J. Absorbing 1100 J while 400 J of work is done on the system gives ΔU = 1500 J.
Limitations: the first law does not tell the direction of heat flow, the conditions under which heat can be converted to work, or how much of it can be.
## Thermodynamic processes
Isothermal (T constant): the process is slow, in a conducting vessel. ΔU = 0, so Q = W, and PV = constant.
Adiabatic (Q = 0): the process is fast, in an insulated vessel. ΔU = −W, and PV^γ = constant. A gas cools when it expands adiabatically, because it does work using its own internal energy.
Isobaric (P constant): the indicator diagram is a horizontal line. Isochoric (V constant): W = 0.

A reversible process can be retraced exactly through the same states, as in very slow frictionless compression. Irreversible processes include friction, free expansion and heat flowing across a temperature difference. All natural processes are irreversible.
## Second law and heat engines
Kelvin–Planck statement: no engine working in a cycle can convert all the heat it takes in into work, so 100% efficiency is impossible.
Clausius statement: heat cannot flow by itself from a colder body to a hotter one.
A heat engine takes Q₁ from a source at T₁, does work W and rejects Q₂ to a sink at T₂. Its efficiency is η = W/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁.

The Carnot engine is an ideal reversible engine. Its cycle is isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression and adiabatic compression. Its efficiency η = 1 − T₂/T₁ (kelvin) is independent of the working substance, and no real engine between T₁ and T₂ can be more efficient.
η = 100% would need T₂ = 0 K, which cannot be reached.
Examples: between the steam point and the ice point, η = 1 − 273/373 ≈ 26.8%. Between 227 °C and 27 °C, η = 40%. With the sink at 27 °C and η = 25%, the source is at 400 K.
A refrigerator is a heat engine run in reverse. Left open in a closed room it warms the room, because it rejects the heat it removes plus the work done by its motor.

vsa: Calculate the change in internal energy when (a) a system absorbs 2000 J of heat and does 500 J of work, (b) a system absorbs 1100 J of heat and 400 J of work is done on it.

ΔU = Q − W (W = work done by the system).
(a) ΔU = 2000 − 500 = 1500 J.
(b) W = −400 J, so ΔU = 1100 + 400 = 1500 J.
April 2026
Why can a Carnot engine never be 100% efficient?
η = 1 − T₂/T₁. For η = 1 the sink would have to be at T₂ = 0 K, which cannot be reached. Some heat must always be rejected to the sink (Kelvin–Planck statement).
April 2026
Name the four strokes of the Carnot cycle in sequence.
(1) Isothermal expansion at T₁ (heat absorbed). (2) Adiabatic expansion (gas cools to T₂). (3) Isothermal compression at T₂ (heat rejected). (4) Adiabatic compression (back to T₁).
April 2025
If the door of a working refrigerator is kept open in a closed room, will the room warm or cool? Explain.
It will warm. The refrigerator takes heat Q₂ from inside and rejects Q₁ = Q₂ + W into the room. With the door open both are in the same room, so the net heat added is W, the electrical energy used.

What is an indicator diagram? Draw it for an isobaric process.

An indicator diagram is a P–V graph showing how the state of a gas changes; the area under it gives the work done. For an isobaric process it is a horizontal straight line at constant P from V₁ to V₂, and W = P(V₂ − V₁).

sa: Distinguish between reversible and irreversible processes with an example of each.

Reversible: can be retraced in the opposite direction through the same states, leaving no change in the surroundings. It must be extremely slow and frictionless. Example: very slow isothermal compression of a gas.
Irreversible: cannot be retraced exactly. Examples: heat flowing from hot to cold, friction producing heat, free expansion of a gas.
All natural processes are irreversible.
State the first law of thermodynamics and its limitations.

First law: ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW — heat supplied raises the internal energy and does external work (conservation of energy).
Limitations: it does not tell (i) the direction of heat flow, (ii) the conditions under which heat can be converted into work, or (iii) how much heat can be converted into work. The second law answers these.
Explain why (a) there is no change in the internal energy of an ideal gas in an isothermal change and (b) an ideal gas cools during adiabatic expansion.

(a) The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature. In an isothermal change T is constant, so ΔU = 0 and all the heat supplied goes into work.
(b) In an adiabatic process Q = 0, so ΔU = −W. During expansion the gas does positive work using its own internal energy, so U falls and the temperature drops.
Calculate the efficiency of a Carnot engine working between 27 °C and 227 °C. If it absorbs 1000 J per cycle, how much work does it do?
la: Explain isothermal and adiabatic processes. Give the conditions for each, draw their indicator diagrams and give one example of each.

Isothermal: temperature stays constant. Conditions: the gas is in a thin, conducting container in contact with a large reservoir, and the change is slow. ΔU = 0, Q = W, PV = constant. On the P–V diagram it is a hyperbola. Example: slow compression of a gas in a metal cylinder; melting of ice at 0 °C.
Adiabatic: no heat exchange (Q = 0). Conditions: the container is well insulated and the change is fast. ΔU = −W, PV^γ = constant. Its curve is steeper than the isothermal. Example: sudden bursting of a tyre (the air cools); compression stroke of a diesel engine.
Describe the construction and working of a Carnot engine. Derive or state its efficiency.

Construction: an ideal cylinder with frictionless, insulating walls and piston, a conducting base, and an ideal gas as working substance; a hot source at T₁, a cold sink at T₂ and an insulating stand.
Working (Carnot cycle):
(1) On the source — isothermal expansion; absorbs Q₁.
(2) On the stand — adiabatic expansion; cools from T₁ to T₂.
(3) On the sink — isothermal compression; rejects Q₂.
(4) On the stand — adiabatic compression; back to T₁.
Net work W = Q₁ − Q₂ = area of the cycle on the P–V diagram.
Efficiency η = 1 − Q₂/Q₁ = 1 − T₂/T₁. It is independent of the working substance and is the highest possible between T₁ and T₂.
State the first law of thermodynamics and the Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements of the second law. Give the importance of each law.

First law: ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW — conservation of energy for thermal processes. Importance: it relates heat, work and internal energy, and shows no machine can produce work without an energy input (no perpetual motion of the first kind).
Kelvin–Planck: no engine working in a cycle can convert all the heat absorbed into work.
Clausius: heat cannot flow by itself from a colder to a hotter body.
Importance of the second law: it gives the direction of natural processes, shows that 100% efficiency is impossible, and is the basis of heat engines and refrigerators.
